A candle is a small fuel system. The **wax** is the fuel, the **wick** is the pump, and the **flame** is the engine. When you light the wick, the heat melts a little wax around it into a shallow liquid called the **melt pool**. The wick soaks up that liquid wax and carries it upward, the same way a cloth soaks up water. This movement through tiny gaps in the wick is called **capillary action**.

Near the top of the wick the heat turns the liquid wax into a hot gas (vapour). That gas mixes with oxygen from the air and burns, giving light, heat, water vapour and carbon dioxide. The heat then melts more wax, and the cycle continues on its own. The National Candle Association explains that all waxes are mostly hydrogen and carbon, which is why they burn this way. If the cycle is broken, for example the wick is too thin to carry enough wax or the flame cannot get enough air, the candle smokes, shrinks or goes out.

Reading the flame

Look closely at a lit candle and you will see colours. The blue part at the bottom is where wax vapour starts to break apart. The bright yellow part is glowing carbon particles: this is where most of the light comes from. The thin outer edge is the hottest part. A flicker that sends up black smoke means some carbon escaped without burning. In your own candles, regular smoke is a sign that something is wrong, usually a wick that is too big or too long, or a draught.

Every wax is sold with a recommended melting, fragrance and pouring temperature. These differ from product to product, so always ask your supplier for the **product data sheet** and keep it in your notebook. Use a thermometer every time. Guessing temperature by eye is the main reason beginners get bad results and the main way kitchens get burnt.
Setting up a safe workspace
Choose a stable table or counter away from curtains, gas cylinders and anything that can burn. Keep the floor clear so you cannot trip while carrying hot wax.

Use a **double boiler**: a large pot with some water, and a metal pouring jug or smaller pot of wax standing inside it. The water stops the wax from getting hotter than boiling water, which protects the wax and lowers the fire risk.
Never put a pot of wax directly on a gas flame, kerosene stove or hot plate, and never leave melting wax unattended, not even for a quick phone call or to answer the gate.
Keep the water level topped up so the outer pot never boils dry, and keep water out of the wax: water in hot wax spits and can burn you.
Keep a metal lid that fits your pot, a fire blanket if you can get one, and oven gloves within arm's reach before you switch on the heat.
Keep children and pets out of the room while wax is hot.
If wax catches fire

Turn off the heat if you can do it safely. Smother the flames by sliding a metal lid or fire blanket over the pot and leave it covered until it is completely cold. **Never pour water on a wax fire**: the water turns to steam instantly and throws burning wax out of the pot. Do not try to carry the burning pot outside. If the fire is not out at once, get everyone out of the house and call for help.

Overheated wax gives warnings before it catches fire. If you see smoke rising from the wax itself, or smell a sharp burning smell, switch off the heat straight away and let it cool. This is why the thermometer matters: if your wax is near the temperature on the data sheet, you are working far below the danger zone.
Worked example: setting up in a small kitchen
For example, Chiamaka in Owerri has a two-burner gas cooker, a 5 litre pot, a 1 litre stainless steel jug and one hour while her children are at school.
She clears the counter next to the cooker, moves the kitchen curtain out of the way, and puts the pot lid and a dry towel nearby.
She pours water into the big pot until it reaches about one third of the way up the jug, so the jug cannot float or tip.
She weighs 500 g of container wax into the jug and places the jug in the water, then lights the burner on medium.
She clips her thermometer to the jug and checks it every few minutes, stirring gently with a metal spoon.
When the doorbell rings, she switches off the burner before going to the gate, then relights it when she returns.
Her wax melts evenly to the temperature on her data sheet, no water gets into the wax, and the cooker is never left burning without her.

The wick decides how a candle behaves more than any other part. The same wax in the same jar can burn beautifully with one wick and badly with another. A wick that is **too small** makes a narrow melt pool, so the candle burns a tunnel down the middle and wastes the wax on the sides. A wick that is **too big** makes a tall flame, smoke and soot, and can make a glass jar dangerously hot.
The common wick types
**Flat braided cotton wicks**: plaited like hair, they curl slightly as they burn. Often used in pillars and tapers.
**Square braided cotton wicks**: thicker and rounder, popular for beeswax and pillar candles.
**Cored wicks**: a cotton wick with a stiffer centre that helps it stand up straight in container candles and tealights. Buy from a supplier who states what the core is made of.
**Wooden wicks**: thin strips of wood that crackle softly. They need their own size chart and practice.

Most container and tealight wicks are sold **pre-tabbed**: a small metal disc called a **wick tab** (or sustainer) is clamped to the bottom. The tab holds the wick in place and stops the flame before it reaches the base of the jar, which protects the glass. Every supplier publishes a **size chart** that matches wick sizes to wax type and container diameter. Use the chart as your starting point, then test. Charts are a guide, not a promise, because your fragrance, dye and jar shape all change the result.
A woman testing samples at a work table
Treat every new jar, wax or fragrance as an experiment and test the wick before you sell.
Fixing a wick in a jar
Wipe the inside of the jar clean and dry. Dust and grease stop the tab from sticking.
Measure the jar's inside diameter at its widest point with a ruler and write it down. This is the number you look up in the wick chart.
Put a wick sticker or a small dot of melted wax on the bottom of the tab and press it to the exact centre of the jar with a pencil or chopstick.
Pull the wick upright and hold it centred with a wick bar, a clothes peg, or two pencils with a rubber band across the jar mouth.
Leave the wick holder in place until the wax is completely set.
The burn test

A burn test is how you prove that your candle is safe and works well. Make at least two test candles with the same wax, fragrance and wick. Let them cure as your wax supplier advises. Then burn one in a still room, on a heat-proof surface, away from fans, open windows and anything that can burn, and stay in the room the whole time.

At each check, write down the time, the flame height, the width of the melt pool, any smoke or soot, and whether the glass feels too hot to hold comfortably near the top. For a container candle, a good result is a melt pool that reaches close to the edge of the jar within a few hours, a calm flame, and no black smoke. Keep the trimmed wick short: the National Candle Association advises trimming wicks to a quarter of an inch (about 6 mm) before each use to prevent high flames and soot.
Worked example: reading a burn test log

For example, Folake in Ibadan makes candles in a jar with an inside diameter of 7.5 cm. She tests two wick sizes from her supplier's chart, one size apart, called size A (smaller) and size B (larger).
After 1 hour, wick A has a melt pool 4.0 cm wide; wick B has a melt pool 5.5 cm wide.
After 2 hours, wick A has 5.5 cm; wick B has 7.0 cm and its flame is calm.
After 3 hours, wick A is still 1 cm short of the edge on each side: 7.5 cm minus 5.5 cm leaves 2.0 cm of solid wax across the jar, so it is starting to tunnel.
Wick B reached 7.0 cm at 2 hours, leaving only 0.5 cm, and closes to the edge by hour 3 with no smoke.
She checks wick B's jar near the rim by touch with the back of her hand: warm, not too hot to hold.
Wick B is the right choice for this jar, wax and fragrance. Folake writes the jar size, wax, fragrance load and wick B in her recipe card so every future batch uses the same combination.

Container candles are poured into glass jars, tins or ceramic cups and burn inside them. They are the best first product to sell: the jar holds the wax, so you can use soft container wax, the candle cannot fall over, and customers like them as gifts. In this lesson you will make a batch of 12 scented jar candles, using numbers you work out yourself rather than guesses.
A glass jar
Choose a jar made for candles: thick, heat-resistant glass with no cracks or chips.
Step 1: Find out how much wax one jar holds

Wax does not weigh the same as water, and every jar is different, so the most accurate method is a **test pour**. Weigh an empty, clean jar on a digital kitchen scale. Melt some wax, pour it to the fill line you want (usually about 1 to 1.5 cm below the rim, so the flame sits inside the glass), and let it set completely. Weigh the jar again. The difference is the wax one jar holds. Write it on your recipe card; you only need to do this once per jar style.
Step 2: Calculate the batch

Multiply the wax per jar by the number of jars. Then add about 5 percent extra, because some wax always stays on the jug and spoon. **Fragrance load** is the amount of fragrance oil, written as a percentage of the wax weight. Your wax supplier's data sheet gives a maximum: never go above it, because extra oil can leak out of the candle (called sweating) and can make it burn unsafely. Many makers test a lower load first and only go higher if the scent is weak.
Worked example: a batch of 12 jars

For example, Halima in Kaduna has 12 identical jars. Her test pour showed the empty jar weighs 210 g and the filled jar weighs 390 g. Her wax data sheet allows the fragrance load she wants to use, and she chooses 6 percent.
Wax per jar: 390 g minus 210 g = 180 g.
Wax for 12 jars: 12 x 180 g = 2,160 g.
Add 5 percent for loss: 2,160 g x 1.05 = 2,268 g of wax to melt.
Fragrance at 6 percent of the wax melted: 2,268 g x 0.06 = 136.08 g, so she weighs out 136 g of fragrance oil.
She writes all four numbers on her batch sheet before she switches on the cooker.
Halima melts 2,268 g of wax and adds 136 g of fragrance oil. She has enough to fill all 12 jars to the line, with a little left for topping up.
Step 3: The method
Wash and dry the jars well. Fix a pre-tabbed wick in the centre of each one and hold it upright with a wick bar or peg.
Warm the jars slightly by standing them in a warm place (not in water). Cold glass can make wax pull away from the sides.
Melt the weighed wax in your double boiler, checking the thermometer, until it reaches the melting temperature on the data sheet.
Add dye if you are using it, and stir until no streaks remain.
Let the wax cool to the fragrance temperature on the data sheet, add the weighed fragrance oil, and stir gently and steadily for about two minutes so it fully mixes in.
When the wax reaches the pouring temperature on the data sheet, pour slowly into each jar to the fill line, keeping the wick centred.
Leave the jars to cool undisturbed in a room without draughts. Do not move them or put them in a fridge.

Step 4: Finish and cure

As wax cools it shrinks, and you may see a dip or small holes around the wick. Reheat a little of the leftover wax and pour a thin top-up layer to make the surface flat. When the candle is completely hard, trim the wick to about 6 mm. Then let the candles **cure**: rest with lids on, at room temperature, so the fragrance settles into the wax. Curing time depends on the wax, so follow the supplier's advice.

A pillar candle stands on its own without a jar. That means the wax must be hard enough to hold its shape when warm, so you use a **pillar grade wax** (a harder paraffin, palm wax, beeswax or a blend made for pillars), not soft container wax. Pillars are popular for church use, table settings, events and gift sets, and a neat, smooth pillar looks very professional.
Choosing a mould
**Metal moulds** (aluminium): last for years and give a smooth, shiny finish. They have a small hole at the bottom for the wick.
**Plastic or polycarbonate moulds**: cheaper and show you the wax through the side, but can be damaged if the wax is hotter than the mould maker allows.
**Silicone moulds**: bend away from the candle, so they are good for shapes such as spheres, cubes and flowers. You push the wick through with a wicking needle.
**Home-made moulds** such as clean cardboard tubes lined with baking paper work for tests, but are hard to make perfectly round.

Remember that the **bottom of the mould becomes the top of the candle**. The wick goes through the hole at the base of the mould, and is tied or clipped across the open end, which becomes the candle's base.
Preparing the mould
Clean and dry the mould. Any old wax or dust shows on the finished surface.
Thread a pillar wick (not pre-tabbed) through the hole in the base, leaving a few centimetres outside.
Seal the hole from the outside with mould sealer putty so no wax leaks out. Press it firmly around the wick.
Pull the wick straight and tie it to a wick bar or pencil resting across the open end, exactly in the centre.
If your mould maker recommends it, wipe the inside with a very thin film of mould release. Silicone moulds usually do not need it.
Stand the mould on a tray on a level surface.
A maker working carefully at a bench
Pillar work rewards patience: a straight wick and slow cooling give the cleanest result.
How much wax to melt

Before your first pour, seal the mould, fill it with water up to the line you want, and weigh the water. A gram of water is about a millilitre, so this tells you the mould's volume. Candle wax is lighter than water, so the wax that fills the same space weighs **less** than the water did. If you melt the same number of grams of wax as the water weighed, you will have enough, with some extra for the second pour. Dry the mould completely before using it for wax.
Worked example: a 7 cm by 10 cm pillar
For example, Ruth in Jos has an aluminium cylinder mould. She fills it with water to 10 cm high, and the water weighs 385 g.
Because wax is lighter than water, 385 g of wax will more than fill the mould. She rounds up and melts 400 g of pillar wax to have enough for both pours.
She uses a 5 percent fragrance load, within her pillar wax data sheet's maximum: 400 g x 0.05 = 20 g of fragrance oil.
She keeps about 60 g of the scented wax back in the jug for the second pour, so the first pour is about 400 g minus 60 g = 340 g.
When a firm skin forms on top, she pokes two or three relief holes near the wick with a skewer to let trapped air out.
Once the candle has shrunk and a dip forms around the wick, she reheats the reserved wax and fills the dip, stopping at the level of the first pour.
The second pour fills the cavity so the base is flat and solid. Ruth records 400 g melted and 60 g reserved on her recipe card for this mould.

Unmoulding and finishing

Wait until the candle is completely cool all the way through. This can take many hours for a large pillar. Remove the putty and untie the wick. A candle that is fully cool shrinks slightly from the mould walls and slides out easily; if it sticks, it usually needs more time. Never force it with a knife, which scratches both mould and candle.

To level the base, rub it gently in small circles on a clean metal tray warmed over your double boiler until the bottom is flat, then let it harden. Trim the wick at the top to about 6 mm. Polish the sides with a soft cloth or a nylon stocking to remove fingerprints.

They use little wax each, so they are cheap to make, but they must be identical, burn safely and be ready on the day promised. This lesson shows you how to produce them in batches, and how to add decorative styles that make your table candles stand out.

Making tealights in bulk
Buy empty tealight cups (aluminium or clear plastic made for candles) and pre-tabbed tealight wicks that match your supplier's chart.
Do a test pour to find how much wax one cup holds, as you did for jars.
Set the cups out in rows on a tray, close together, so you can pour along a line.
Place a wick tab in the centre of each cup. Many tealight wicks stand on their own; if not, press the tab down with a pencil.
Pour from a jug with a narrow spout, filling each cup just below the rim. Re-centre any wick that tilts while the wax is still liquid.
Leave to set, then top up any dips with a little reheated wax.

For example, Grace in Benin City receives an order for 48 unscented white tealights for a naming ceremony on Saturday. Her test pour showed one cup holds 14 g of wax.
Wax needed: 48 x 14 g = 672 g.
Add 5 percent for loss: 672 g x 1.05 = 705.6 g, so she melts about 706 g.
Unscented is better for food tables, so she adds no fragrance oil.
She makes 50, not 48, so she can keep two for a short burn test before delivery.

Events need many identical candles delivered on time, so plan quantities and dates backwards from the event.
Votives

Votives are made in small metal votive moulds, using a wick with its own small tab, and a wax suitable for votives. When burned, a well-wicked votive melts completely and becomes a pool of liquid wax, so it must burn in a glass or metal holder only slightly larger than the candle. Tell customers this clearly: a votive on a bare plate will spread hot wax across the table.
Decorative techniques

**Layered candles**: pour one colour, let it set until the surface is firm but still warm, then pour the next colour. Pouring too early makes the colours mix; waiting until the first layer is cold can make the layers separate.
**Ombre (colour grading)**: start with lightly coloured wax for the first layer, then add a little more dye to the jug before each next layer, so the colour deepens from bottom to top.
**Wax chunk candles**: pour coloured pillar wax into a tray, cut the hardened wax into cubes, place them in a mould, and pour clear or white wax over them.
**Tilted layers**: prop jars at an angle with a folded towel while each layer sets for a slanted stripe effect.
Keep decorations away from the flame

Dried flowers, leaves, herbs, paper, ribbons and glitter can catch fire. Do not put them in the wax that the flame will reach. Decorate the **outside** of the jar, the lid, the label or the gift box instead. Keep coloured wax chunks and dye as your decoration inside the candle.

Colour is easy to overdo. Liquid wax always looks darker than it will when set, and too much dye can affect how a candle burns. Add a small amount, stir, then drip a little on a white saucer to see the true colour once it cools. Write down exactly how many chips or drops gave the shade you want so the next batch matches.

For example, Nkechi in Abuja sells a jar candle called 'Warm Vanilla'. A customer sends a WhatsApp photo: after the third burn, there is a deep tunnel and the flame is small. The batch code on the base is NK-14.

Your label is where a customer decides whether to trust you. It must tell her what she is buying, how to use it safely, and how to reach you. A clean, honest label also makes your candles easier to sell to shops, hotels and event planners, who need to know exactly what they are stocking.
What goes on a candle label
**Brand name and logo**, the same on every product.
**Product name and scent**, for example 'Garden Fresh: lemongrass, ginger and vanilla'.
**Net weight of wax** in grams, from your test pour (not the weight of the jar).
**Wax type**, described honestly. Only say '100% soy' if the wax really is 100 percent soy.

Safety wording you can use

Based on National Candle Association guidance: Never leave a burning candle unattended. Keep out of reach of children and pets. Keep at least 30 cm (12 inches) from anything that can burn. Trim the wick to about 6 mm (1/4 inch) before each use. Stop using when about 1.3 cm (1/2 inch) of wax remains. Put out with a snuffer or by blowing gently, never with water.
Testing burn time

Do not guess burn time or copy it from another brand. Take two finished, cured candles from the same batch. Burn each in sessions of a few hours, in a still room, while you stay with it. Write the start and stop time of every session. Trim the wick before each session. Stop when about 1.3 cm of wax remains, then add up the hours. Use the **lower** of the two results and round down, so customers get at least what you promise.

She takes the lower result, 16.5 hours, and rounds down.
Her label says 'Burn time: about 16 hours'.
Every customer's candle should last at least as long as the label says, so Halima's claim is honest and she has a written test log to back it up.

Many makers price candles by looking at what others charge, then discover months later that they were working for free. The safe way is to cost every batch from your own receipts, then add a profit you choose. In this lesson all naira figures are **made-up example prices** to show the method. Prices change often, so always use your own current receipts.
Step 1: Cost the whole batch

List everything that goes into the batch: wax, fragrance, wicks, jars, dye, labels, boxes and the gas or electricity you use. Then add your **labour**: the hours you spend multiplied by a fair hourly rate. If you leave out your own time, your price will be too low to grow the business. Finally, remember the candles you keep for burn tests: they cost money but are not sold.
Worked example: costing Halima's batch of 12 jars
For example, Halima uses her batch HK-07 numbers (2,268 g wax, 136 g fragrance, 12 jars). The prices below are example figures only.
Wax: 2.268 kg x 4,000 naira per kg = 9,072 naira.
Fragrance: 136 g x 30 naira per g = 4,080 naira.
Wicks: 12 x 150 = 1,800 naira. Jars: 12 x 600 = 7,200 naira.
Dye 300 naira; labels 12 x 100 = 1,200 naira; gift boxes 12 x 250 = 3,000 naira; gas 800 naira.
Labour: 4 hours x 1,000 naira = 4,000 naira. Batch total: 27,452 + 4,000 = 31,452 naira.
She keeps 1 candle for burn testing, so 11 are for sale: 31,452 / 11 = about 2,859 naira per candle.
Each candle Halima sells really costs her about 2,859 naira (example figures). Any price below this loses money, even if the candles sell fast.
Step 2: Set the price with a margin

**Profit margin** is the share of the selling price that is profit. To get a price with a chosen margin, divide the cost by (1 minus the margin). For a 40 percent margin: 2,859 / 0.60 = about 4,765 naira. Halima rounds up to a clean **4,800 naira**. Her profit per candle is 4,800 minus 2,859 = 1,941 naira, which is about 40 percent of the price. If 11 candles sell, the batch brings in 11 x 4,800 = 52,800 naira, and after the full batch cost of 31,452 naira (which already pays her labour), 21,348 naira is left as profit.

Why this matters
A candle is a small fuel system
Wax is the fuel
The wick is the pump
The flame is the engine
Break the cycle and it smokes or goes out
Think of a candle as a small fuel system. The wax is the fuel.
The wick is the pump. Heat melts wax into a shallow melt pool, and the wick soaks it up like a cloth soaks up water.
The flame is the engine. The wax turns to hot gas at the top of the wick and burns, and that heat melts more wax.
If the wick is too thin or the flame lacks air, the candle smokes, shrinks or goes out.
Know your wax
Paraffin: containers, pillars, tealights
Soy wax: soft, made for jars
Palm wax: hard, for pillars and votives
Beeswax: premium, needs a larger wick
Paraffin is widely available and usually cheapest.
Soy wax is soft, so most of it is made for jars.
Palm wax is hard, good for pillars and votives.
Beeswax costs more and needs a larger wick.
For any wax, ask your supplier for the product data sheet with its temperatures, and use a thermometer every time. Guessing by eye is the main reason beginners get bad results.
Step by step
Set up a safe melting station
Never put wax straight on the flame. Never leave it alone.
Stable table, away from curtains and gas cylinders
Use a double boiler: wax jug inside a pot of water
Top up the water; keep water out of the wax
Lid, fire blanket and oven gloves within reach
Children and pets out of the room
Step 1. Work at a stable table away from curtains, gas cylinders and anything that can burn.
Step 2. Use a double boiler: a large pot of water with your metal jug of wax standing inside. The water stops the wax getting hotter than boiling water.
Step 3. Keep the water topped up, and keep water out of the wax, because it spits and burns.
Step 4. Put a fitting metal lid and oven gloves within reach before you switch on the heat.
Step 5. Children and pets stay out.
The rule: never put wax directly on a gas flame or stove, and never leave melting wax alone, not even to answer the gate.
Emergency
Turn off the heat if safe. Slide a metal lid or fire blanket over the pot. Leave it until cold.
Water turns to steam at once and throws burning wax out of the pot. Do not carry the pot outside.
If the fire is not out at once, get everyone out of the house and call for help.
If wax catches fire, turn off the heat if it is safe, and slide a metal lid or fire blanket over the pot. Leave it covered until cold.
Never pour water on a wax fire. It turns to steam and throws burning wax out of the pot.
If the fire is not out at once, get everyone out and call for help.
Worked example
Folake's burn test: wick A or B?
Wick A (smaller)
1 hour: pool 4.0 cm
2 hours: pool 5.5 cm
3 hours: still short, tunnelling
Wick B (larger)
1 hour: pool 5.5 cm
2 hours: 7.0 cm, calm flame
3 hours: full pool, no smoke
The wick decides how a candle behaves. Too small, and it burns a tunnel. Too big, and you get soot and a hot jar. So you test.
For example, Folake in Ibadan has a jar 7.5 cm wide. She tries 2 wick sizes next to each other on her supplier's chart.
Wick A makes a melt pool of 4.0 cm after 1 hour and 5.5 cm after 2 hours. At 3 hours it is still short of the edge, and starting to tunnel.
Wick B reaches 7.0 cm at 2 hours with a calm flame, and the full edge by hour 3 with no smoke. Wick B wins, and she writes it on a recipe card.
Burn test safely
Every test candle
Stay in the room the whole time
Metal tray or ceramic plate, no draughts
Trim the wick to about 6 mm
Put it out with a snuffer, never water
Stop when about 1.3 cm of wax is left
Test safely. Stay in the room, and burn on a metal tray or ceramic plate away from draughts. Trim the wick to about 6 mm. Use a snuffer, never water. Stop when about 1.3 cm of wax is left.

Remember
The wick carries melted wax up to the flame
Follow each wax's data sheet and use a thermometer
Double boiler, and never leave wax alone
Wax fire: lid or fire blanket, never water

What you will make
Three product families that sell
Scented jar candles: the best first product
Pillars: stand alone, look professional
Tealights and votives: sold by the dozen
Numbers you work out, not guesses
Most candle businesses sell three families. Jar candles are the best first product: the jar holds the wax, the candle cannot fall over, and customers love them as gifts.
Pillars stand on their own, so they need a harder pillar grade wax.
Tealights and votives sell in quantity for weddings, naming ceremonies and church services.
For all three, you will work out your quantities with real numbers, not guesses.
Worked example
Halima's batch of 12 jars
Never go above the fragrance maximum on your data sheet.
Test pour: full 390 g minus empty 210 g = 180 g
Add 5 percent for loss: 2,268 g of wax
Fragrance at 6 percent: about 136 g
For example, Halima in Kaduna has 12 identical jars. First she does a test pour, because every jar is different.
The empty jar weighs 210 g. Filled with set wax to the line, it weighs 390 g. So one jar holds 180 g of wax.
For 12 jars, that is 12 times 180, which is 2,160 g.
Some wax always stays on the jug and spoon, so she adds about 5 percent. 2,160 times 1.05 gives 2,268 g to melt.
Fragrance load means fragrance oil as a percentage of the wax weight. She chooses 6 percent, so 2,268 times 0.06 gives about 136 g of oil.
Never go above your supplier's maximum. Extra oil can leak out, which is called sweating, and can make the candle burn unsafely.
Step by step
Pouring the jar candles
The thermometer stays in the jug all the way through.
Fix and centre a wick in each clean jar
Warm the jars slightly, not in water
Melt wax to the data sheet temperature
Add dye, then fragrance at its temperature
Pour slowly to the fill line
Cool without draughts; top up and cure
Wash and dry the jars, then fix a pre-tabbed wick in the centre of each one.
Warm the jars slightly in a warm place. Cold glass can make wax pull away from the sides.
Melt the weighed wax in your double boiler to the melting temperature on the data sheet.
Stir in any dye. Let the wax cool to the fragrance temperature, add the oil, and stir gently for about two minutes.
At the pouring temperature, pour slowly to the fill line, keeping the wick centred.
Let them cool where there is no draught, and never in a fridge. Fill any dip with a thin top-up layer, trim the wick to about 6 mm, and let the candles cure before you sell.
Pillar method
Pillars: shrinkage is part of the method
Fill the sealed mould with water and weigh it. Melt that many grams of wax: it is enough.
Keep some wax back. When a firm skin forms, poke relief holes near the wick.
Fill the dip with the reserved wax. Unmould only when fully cool. Never force it.
Now pillars.
The bottom of the mould becomes the top of the candle.
To know how much wax to melt, fill the sealed mould with water and weigh it.
Wax is lighter than water, so the same grams of wax will be enough.
For example, Ruth in Jos melts 400 g of pillar wax and keeps about 60 g back. When a firm skin forms on the first pour, she pokes two or three relief holes near the wick to let trapped air out.
As it shrinks, a dip forms. She reheats the reserved wax and fills it. That is the second pour, not a repair. She waits until it is completely cool, and it slides out easily.
Event candles
Tealight or votive?
A tealight is poured into its own small cup and burns inside it, so you can make them fast in rows on a tray.
For example, Grace in Benin City needs 48 tealights.
Each cup holds 14 g, so she melts about 706 g, and makes 50 so she can burn test two before delivery.
A votive melts into a pool of liquid wax, so it must burn in a holder only slightly larger than the candle. Tell customers clearly, or hot wax will spread across the table.
Before you pour
Event orders and decoration safety
How many, colour and scent, in writing
Delivery date and address
Does the venue allow open flames?
Price and deposit agreed in the same message
Flowers, ribbon, glitter: outside only
Before you accept an event order, ask in writing: how many, what colour and scent, the delivery date and address, and whether the venue allows open flames.
Agree the price and deposit in the same message.
And keep dried flowers, paper, ribbons and glitter out of the wax the flame will reach. Decorate the jar, lid or box instead.
Key points
Remember
A test pour gives the true wax weight
Wax per jar x jars, plus about 5 percent
Fragrance never above the supplier's maximum
Pillars: relief holes and a second pour
Votives always burn in a holder
To remember. Test pour first. Multiply, then add about 5 percent. Keep fragrance within the maximum. Give every pillar relief holes and a second pour. And votives always burn in a holder.

Why this matters
Customers decide by smell in seconds
Cold throw: scent before lighting
Hot throw: scent while it burns
Only oils made for candles
Keep each Safety Data Sheet
Many customers pick up a candle, smell it, and decide in seconds. Cold throw is how strong it smells before it is lit.
Hot throw is how well the scent fills a room while it burns. A good candle has both.
Buy oils described as suitable for candles. Never use perfume, body spray or cooking flavourings: they are not made to burn.
Ask your supplier for the Safety Data Sheet for each oil, and keep them in a folder. Serious buyers such as hotels may ask for them.
Building a blend
The three notes of a scent
Top: lemon, orange, lemongrass, mint
Middle: rose, jasmine, cinnamon, ginger
Base: vanilla, sandalwood, amber, musk
Perfumers describe a scent in three layers called notes. Top notes are the bright smells you notice first, like lemongrass. They fade fastest.
Middle notes are the heart of the scent, often floral or spicy, like ginger.
Base notes are deep and last long, like vanilla. A balanced blend uses some of each, usually with less of the strongest base note.
Worked example
Blessing scales her blend
Test small first. Never go above the supplier's maximum.
Test blend 5 : 3 : 2, about 10 g in total
1,500 g wax x 0.06 = 90 g fragrance
Shares: 50, 30 and 20 percent
45 g lemongrass, 27 g ginger, 18 g vanilla
Plan your blend in parts out of 10, and mix a small test first. For example, Blessing in Port Harcourt likes lemongrass, ginger and vanilla in the ratio 5 to 3 to 2.
She will melt 1,500 g of wax at a 6 percent fragrance load, which is within her data sheet maximum. That gives 90 g of fragrance in total.
5, 3 and 2 make 10 parts, so the shares are 50 percent, 30 percent and 20 percent.
So she weighs 45 g of lemongrass, 27 g of ginger and 18 g of vanilla.
She always checks the total adds back to 90 g.
More fragrance is not always better. Extra oil can seep out, make the flame smoky, or create a fire risk. If the scent is weak, check your wick, temperature and cure time first.
Colour
Colouring wax the right way
Use
Candle dye chips, liquid or flakes
Add dye before fragrance
Test a drip on a white saucer
Record chips per 1,000 g of wax
Never use
Crayons or craft paint
Pigment powders for other crafts
Use dyes made for candles.
Add dye when the wax is fully melted, before the fragrance, and stir until there are no streaks.
Drip a little on a white saucer to see the true colour.
Write down exactly how many chips you used so every batch matches.
Never use crayons or craft paint, because the particles clog the wick and make it smoke. And food colouring is water-based, so it will not mix with wax.
Fault guide
Three faults you will meet
Deep hole, wax left on the sides. Wick too small or first burn too short. Test one size up.
Carbon blob or black smoke. Wick too big or untrimmed. Trim to about 6 mm; test smaller.
Oily drops on top. Too much fragrance or warm storage. Lower the load, store cool.
Most burning faults trace back to the wick, trimming or fragrance load. Tunnelling is a deep hole down the middle. The wick is too small, or the first burn was too short.
Mushrooming is a black blob on the wick tip, often with soot. Trim to about 6 mm before each burn, and test a smaller wick.
Sweating is oily drops on the surface. Lower the fragrance load and store cool.
Wet spots and frosting are mostly about looks. But very high flames, heavy smoke or a glass too hot to touch are safety faults. Stop selling that batch until you have tested a fix.
Nkechi answers a complaint
Change one thing at a time, then burn test again.
Photo of the fault and the batch code
Ask: how long was the first burn?
Check the batch record for changes
Test old wick against one size up
Fix the recipe and update the label
For example, Nkechi in Abuja gets a WhatsApp photo of her Warm Vanilla candle with a deep tunnel. The batch code on the base is NK-14.
She thanks the customer and asks one question. The first burn lasted only about 40 minutes.
Her batch record shows one change: a wider jar, 8.5 cm instead of 7.5 cm, so the old wick is probably too small.
She burns two test candles side by side. The larger wick reaches the edge in about 3 hours. The old one leaves about 1.5 cm of solid wax on each side.
She replaces the customer's candle, uses the larger wick for the wider jar, and adds a label line: let the first burn melt to the edges. Change only one thing at a time, so you know what worked.

Build trust
What goes on your candle label
Brand, product name and scent
Net wax weight in grams
Honest wax type
Batch code and WhatsApp number
Safety and care instructions
Your label is where a customer decides to trust you. Put your brand, product name and scent on the front.
Give the net weight of the wax from your test pour, not the weight of the jar.
Describe the wax honestly. Only say 100% soy if it really is.
Give a burn time from your own timed test, never copied from another brand.

Add your batch code and phone number, and the safety text: never leave a burning candle unattended, keep it 30 cm from anything that can burn, trim the wick to about 6 mm, and put it out with a snuffer, never water.
Worked example
Halima tests burn time
Use the lower result and round down.
Burn 2 cured candles from one batch
Record start and stop of every session
Stop when about 1.3 cm of wax is left
Candle 1: 16.5 hours. Candle 2: 17 hours
Label: about 16 hours
For example, Halima takes two cured candles from batch HK-07.
She burns them in sessions of a few hours while she stays at home, writing the start and stop time each time, and trimming the wick before each session.
She stops when about 1.3 cm of wax remains, then adds up the hours.
Candle 1 burned for 16.5 hours. Candle 2 burned for 17 hours.
She takes the lower result and rounds down, so her label says about 16 hours. Every customer gets at least what she promises.
Packaging
Pack for the buyer
Box with paper filling, ribbon outside the box, and a care card. It must arrive unbroken.
Matching sets with custom labels. Every piece identical, delivered on time.
Plain pillars or tealights in dozens, or a clean jar. Steady quality and supply.
Match the packaging to the buyer. A gift buyer wants a box with paper filling, the ribbon on the outside of the box, and a care card.
An event host wants matching sets, every piece identical, delivered on time.
Churches want plain pillars or tealights packed in dozens. Hotels want a simple clean jar and steady quality.
Candles soften in heat, so store stock in a cool shaded room, and pack jars upright with padding.
Costing Halima's batch of 12 jars
For example, Halima costs batch HK-07: 12 jars, using example prices only.
Wax, 2.268 kg
Fragrance, 136 g
All materials together
Labour, 4 hours
Example figures only. Use your own receipts.
Many makers copy other people's prices and find out months later they were working for free. So cost every batch from your own receipts. These naira figures are example prices only.
Halima's wax costs 9,072 naira and her fragrance 4,080 naira.
With wicks, jars, dye, labels, gift boxes and gas, all her materials come to 27,452 naira.
Then she adds her labour: 4 hours at 1,000 naira. If you leave out your own time, your price will be too low to grow.
The batch total is 31,452 naira. She keeps 1 candle for burn testing, so 11 are for sale. That is about 2,859 naira per candle. Any price below that loses money.
Set the price
From cost to price
Know your floor before you agree any discount.
Cost per candle: about 2,859 naira
40 percent margin: 2,859 / 0.60 = about 4,765
Round up to 4,800 naira
Profit: 1,941 naira per candle
Wholesale at 25 percent off: 3,600, profit 741
Profit margin is the share of the selling price that is profit.
To get a 40 percent margin, divide the cost by 0.60. That gives about 4,765 naira.
Halima rounds up to a clean 4,800 naira.
Her profit is 1,941 naira per candle.
A gift shop asks for 25 percent off.
The price drops to 3,600 naira, and her profit to just 741.
That can be worth it for a large regular order, but not for three candles.
So set a minimum order for wholesale.
Before you release any candles
Check your own bank or payment app
Never trust a screenshot or SMS alert
Deposit first for custom event orders
Record date, buyer, item, amount, how paid
Before you release goods, check that the money is in your own account, in your own bank, Opay or Moniepoint app.
Fake alerts are a common scam, so do not trust a screenshot or an SMS sent by the buyer.
Take a deposit for custom orders, and keep a simple sales record.
Key points
Remember
Label net weight, honest wax, tested burn time
Use the lower burn time, rounded down
Cost the full batch, including your labour
Price = cost divided by (1 minus margin)
Release goods only when you see the money
To remember.
Keep your label honest and tested.
Cost the whole batch, including packaging, gas, your labour and your test candles.
Divide by 1 minus your margin, then round.
And release goods only after the money is in your own account.
